newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF may link Bulgaria loans to 1996 reform targets.
newsitem.headline: IMF may link Bulgaria loans to 1996 reform targets.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund may ask Bulgaria to complete reforms pledged last year, before a fixed exchange rate regime designed to restore confidence in the economy is introduced, an IMF official said on Wednesday.

"It is very likely that the Fund will complete negotiations on the introduction of a currency board with the new government but will link funding approval to fulfilment of reform targets in Bulgaria's previous agreement with the IMF," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
The IMF is expected to complete talks on the implementation of the currency board system after parliament approves a new Socialist government by mid-January.
The Socialists are discussing with their parliamentary allies the nomination of Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev as prime minister.

Under a funding agreement sealed with the Fund in July last year Bulgaria pledged to speed up privatisation, shut down 64 loss-making state enterprises and curb lending for a further 70 inefficient but essential state firms like the state railways, power and heating plants.
The IMF and the World Bank suspended funding because of the Socialist government's failure to reduce budget draining subsidies and boost revenue through sell-offs.

In November the IMF proposed the introduction of the currency board system, which severely curbs the financial powers of the government and the central bank, to boost confidence in the crumbling financial system.
Up to one billion dollars in savings were withdrawn from Bulgaria's ailing banks last year, the central bank said.
On Tuesday Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said Bulgaria would be able to introduce a curency board system by the end of February if the technical preparations were speeded up.

However government officials and some central bankers have said the hurried preparation of the currency board has many flaws and its introduction, if sustainable, would not be possible before March or even April.
Preparations include restructuring the central bank to four departments, passing a viable 1997 budget in parliament and approving legal amendments to banking laws.
The central bank has already taken the first step towards restricting the lev's volatility by changing the method of the daily currency fixing calculations.
As from Monday the bank will calculate lev/dollar fixings when daily interbank turnover is higher than $20 million. Bulgaria's illiquid interbank foreign exchange market is moved by small volumes.
The daily lev/dollar fix has remained unchanged at 581.78 in the past three days, although on the interbank market the lev traded at around 640 to the dollar.
Parliament is also expected to decide to which currency to peg the lev, the dollar or the mark. -- Elisaveta Konstantinova, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
